newsitem.title: POLAND: New rain threatens more floods in central Europe.
newsitem.headline: New rain threatens more floods in central Europe.

text.p: Rain lashed Poland and the Czech Republic anew on Friday, threatening a ruinous new wave in flooding that has already killed 94 people and wrecked many thousands of homes and businesses.

Cloudbursts from the same general low-pressure system battered neighbouring Austria as well, putting wide areas of the country on flood alert as swollen rivers rose to the verge of spilling over their banks.

The new precipitation tormenting Poles and Czechs was not as intense as at the outset of the two-week-old flood crisis but the ground was now so soggy and rivers so high that they could scarcely absorb any more water, officials said.

"The rains are dangerous even though we estimate they will be only one third of the great downpours which hit us over a dozen days ago," said Krzysztof Szamalek, a deputy environment minister on the crisis committee told public radio.

In the Czech Republic, where flood tides have left 46 dead in the country's worst natural calamity this century, light rain started falling from the middle of the night in the worst-hit eastern region including Moravia.
Water levels had been receding but were likely to resurge with the new rain forecast to continue over the weekend.
River authorities emptied dams on the Vltava, which runs through the capital Prague, and on other rivers to make way for the expected downpour.
Polish flood crisis committee spokesman Krzysztof Pomes said the rain was pelting a swathe of western Poland from the Baltic coast in the north to mountains in the south.
Parliament, sitting deep into the night, passed more than 20 bills allowing the government to increase borrowing and rush both funds and rescue assistance to smitten areas.

High finance was far from the minds of exhausted Poles who faced a repeat of the nightmare that swamped more than 4,000 sq km of land and 970 towns and villages, leaving a shroud of filth and the risk of epidemic in its wake.
Flags were at half mast, churches held services, public broadcasters played serious music to mark a day of mourning for the 48 people killed so far in the inundation.
In Austria, meteorologist Manfred Bauer predicted a flood catastrophe if downpours kept up in the regions of Lower Austria, Styria, Salzburg and Upper Austria.
